description: Think you know your music? Come put it to the test at Russian Speaking Society’s Muzloto Night! You’ll get a card with 25 song titles, and as songs play, your goal is to identify them and mark them off. Guess 20 songs correctly to win. title: What's The Word?
description: Description: “What’s the Word?” is a facilitated conversation and community-building space for men of colour at Boston University. The event is designed to provide a welcoming and supportive environment where students can openly discuss topics and experiences that affect their communities, including campus life, identity, personal development, relationships, academics, and professional growth. Through guided discussions and informal conversation, participants will have the opportunity to build fellowship and camaraderie, develop meaningful connections, and foster mentorship between members of the community. The overall goal of “What’s the Word?” is to create a space where men of colour at BU can feel comfortable sharing their perspectives, supporting one another, building a stronger sense of belonging, and developing lasting connections within the university community. How is this event aligned with Howard Thurman’s philosophies? “What’s the Word?” aligns closely with Howard Thurman’s philosophy of searching for common ground through self-understanding, meaningful dialogue, and genuine connection with others. The event creates a space centred on the experiences of men of colour and other underrepresented communities at Boston University, where students can openly discuss topics affecting their identities, communities, relationships, academic experiences, and personal development. Through these conversations, attendees are encouraged to better understand their own experiences while also listening to and learning from the perspectives of others. In doing so, the event promotes fellowship, empathy, mentorship, and a stronger sense of community, reflecting Thurman’s belief that meaningful shared experiences can help overcome the barriers that separate people. How will it create an experience of self-exploration and connection for the attendees? This event will create opportunities for self-exploration through guided and open-ended conversations that encourage participants to reflect on their identities, experiences, challenges, goals, and roles within their communities. Attendees will have opportunities to share their perspectives while hearing from others who may have similar or different experiences. These discussions are intended not only to encourage personal reflection, but also to help students recognise common experiences and develop meaningful relationships. This directly reflects the Howard Thurman Centre’s emphasis on discovering oneself through interaction and connection with others. How will the event organiser attract a reasonable amount of attendees to fill the space being requested? We will promote these events through social media, group chats, flyers, word of mouth, and outreach to other student organisations and affinity groups. By combining broad campus promotion with personal outreach from members, Brothers United aims to reach students beyond its current membership and encourage strong participation in the event.

title: First-Gen Support Group
description: This group offers a safe and supportive space for students who identify as a first-generation college student. Topics discussed may include navigating unfamiliar situations, balancing academics with social life, managing responsibilities and finances, and processing feelings, such as excitement, guilt, shame, confusion and pride. The group emphasizes building community supports and sharing resources. The group is lead by a licensed clinical social worker, Rashidat, who was a first-generation college graduate along with a first-gen graduate student in a BU counseling program. title: First-Gen Support Group
description: This group offers a safe and supportive space for students who identify as a first-generation college student. Topics discussed may include navigating unfamiliar situations, balancing academics with social life, managing responsibilities and finances, and processing feelings, such as excitement, guilt, shame, confusion and pride. The group emphasizes building community supports and sharing resources. The group is lead by a licensed clinical social worker, Rashidat, who was a first-generation college graduate along with a first-gen graduate student in a BU counseling program. What does it mean to be first-generation at Boston University? First-Generation College Student (FGCS): A student in the first generation of their family to go to college (i.e., a student whose parents/guardians/caregivers did not earn bachelor’s degrees, although elder siblings and cousins may be attending college already or have earned four-year degrees). First-Generation Graduate/Professional Student (FGGS/FGPS): A student who is in the first-generation of their families to pursue an advanced degree (i.e., a student whose parents/guardians/caregivers did not earn a master’s, doctorate, or professional degree, such as a JD or MD).

title: October Town Hall
description: The Student Government Town Hall is a single-day event held once a month during the last week of each month and typically lasts one hour. Each session is scheduled for the evening to maximize accessibility, with an expected attendance of 50-75 students depending on the month and topic. The event features catered food, an informational presentation from the Sexual Assault Prevention Department, introductions from SARP, BU Police, and Student Health Services, and a structured discussion format that includes moderated questions and open student Q&A. The most important features of the Town Halls are their consistency, accessibility through rotating weekdays, and the opportunity for direct dialogue between students and decision-makers, ensuring that student perspectives are heard and acted upon.

title: Carnival Latino
description: Carnival Latino (formerly known as Festival Latino) is our first major event of the year making it one of the most important. This event will be our final event for the month of September, which is also Hispanic Heritage Month. Hispanic Heritage Month is tremendously important to the Hispanic community and BU students alike. As the biggest Latinx Association on campus we will hold Festival Latino to gather all Latinx clubs and its members here at BU and give them a space to interact with one another and celebrate the Hispanic community. Additionally, the process of meeting people and finding your home away from home can often be overwhelming. We hope to minimize the hassle by allowing new BU students from all organizations to catch a glimpse of the Latino community in a fun and informative way. At this event we not only invite other BU clubs but also host local Latino artists from the greater Boston area to perform along with some performances from dance groups on campus like Sabor Latino. Tickets will cost $5 dollars to BU students. We will open this event to non-BU students as well, charging them $7 each to attend. The food will be from the beloved Guatemalan restaurant chain, Pollo Campero, and the variety of activities such as face paint, carnival outdoor games, and piñata will be representative of a traditional Latino festival. By holding this event, we hope to encourage students to meet and join our Latinx clubs regardless of background to celebrate Hispanic heritage and embark their BU journey with a strong support system!

title: Every Voice Speaks
description: This program will promote voter participation, civic engagement, and Black political empowerment through the A Voteless People Is A Hopeless People and Foster the Future: From Here to Hope initiatives. The first portion of the program will consist of voter registration and voter education tabling in a low-income community in either Mattapan or Dorchester. Members will help community residents register to vote and provide accessible voter education resources. The evening program, Beyond the Ballot, will focus on civic engagement within the Black community beyond voting. Attendees will learn about additional ways to create change within their communities, including advocacy, contacting elected officials, attending public meetings, community organizing, serving on local boards and commissions, and other forms of civic participation. The program will emphasize that voting is an important component of civic engagement while encouraging attendees to remain involved in their communities beyond Election Day.

The celebration is open to BU students and members of the wider Boston community.
